===== authoringDoctrine
## Components are the unit of good work

**The order comes first.** Settle the look and the screen list before you decide what the components
are — the design doctrine's §"The order" says how, and it is not optional sequencing advice. A
component tree is a decomposition of a list of screens, so a tree decided before that list exists is
a guess; and a look decided after the components is a repaint of every one of them, which is a thing
nobody ever actually does.

Factoring is the default. A page assembled from named section components is easier to read, review
and change than the same page as one long column of nodes.

- **A named section is a component.** Hero, nav, card, form, footer, filter bar. If you would name it
  out loud, it gets its own component and the page instantiates it.
- **Repetition is data.** Two or more structurally identical siblings become one component driven by
  a Repeater over a data source. Never duplicate a subtree by hand.
- **Logic clusters are components.** Three or more logic nodes cooperating on one job get their own
  component with a declared interface, rather than sitting beside the visual nodes.
- **Shared or long code is a script file.** Code two Functions need, or a Function body long enough
  that you would change one line of it, goes in `scripts/<name>.js` (`write_script_file`), listed
  under the Function's `uses` and called as `Scripts.<name>`. `edit_script_file` then changes one
  line without sending the file again; a Function's own code can only be replaced whole.
- **Interfaces are deliberate.** Component Inputs/Outputs carry what varies per instance. Shared app
  state goes through Variables and Objects, not through prop drilling. A component's own state never
  does: a Variable is one value however many times the component is placed, so two copies share it.
- **Placement.** Used once, next to its page. Used twice or plausibly reusable, in a shared folder.
- **Say why on the node.** A node's `label` says what it is for; its `comment` says why it is the way
  it is. Write one where the next reader would otherwise change something and break it — a decision that
  had an alternative, a rule from outside the app that the graph cannot state, or a trap. Omit it when
  the type and label already say it: a comment restating either is noise, and most nodes need none.
- **A named utility is a component however small it is.** A Function that turns a name into
  "A. Surname", a permission check, a date format, a string the API wants in a shape nobody
  remembers — if a builder on another page would rewrite it rather than find it, give it a name and
  a folder. This is the most reused thing in real Noodl codebases and it is usually ONE working
  node: LearnBook's shared logic folders hold 37 such components instantiated 107 times, with
  `Format full name`, `Is Trainer check` and `Generate Google icon object` at nine uses each; 45 of
  the 80 logic-only components the original team shipped in `library/prefabs` are one or two working
  nodes. Findability is the case and reuse is the bonus — a named `Sanitise email` in a shared
  folder is the second builder's answer, an anonymous Function on page 4 is not.

**When not to.** An unnamed wrapper, or a two-node group used once and doing nothing you would say
out loud, is not a component — it is a file and a hop that bought nothing. A page with one section
has one section. ⚠️ **Size is not the test, and a small graph is not the exception.** The test is
whether the thing has a name a person would use; if it does, extract it at one node, and if it does
not, three nodes will not save it.

**Rule of thumb.** A component graph past ~25 nodes is telling you it wanted to be several.
===== interfaceDoctrine
## What goes on a component's interface

You know what becomes a component. This is the other half — what its interface carries — and it is
the half that decides whether the next person can use the thing you built.

**Why this is written down.** Across the examples an agent learns from, **38%** of components publish
any `Component Outputs`. Across the components the original Noodl team shipped in the prefab
library, **84%** do. That gap is the whole difference between a part and a display sink: a sink takes
text, draws it in one fixed place, and tells nobody anything, so every wire it should have owned ends
up back on the page around it — including a wrapper `Group` whose only job is to push it into
position.

**A component someone is glad to inherit is placeable, configurable, and able to say what happened to
it.** The ten patterns below are how that is done, at wire level.

### 1. The placement contract — say how you sit in your parent
Expose your own box: `Align X`, `Align Y`, `Margin Top/Right/Bottom/Left`, `Position`,
`Width`, `Mounted`. Almost every prefab exposes exactly this block — `Toggle Switch`,
`Date Picker`, `Tab Bar`, `Pagination`, `Rating`. Skip it and the parent wraps every instance
in a single-child `Group` that exists for nothing but spacing, which is a node the page keeps
forever and a decision the component should have owned.

### 2. The controlled value — the same name arrives and leaves, plus a change signal
`Toggle Switch` takes `State` and publishes `State` and `State Changed`. `Date Picker`:
`Value` in, `Value` + `Changed` out. `Tab Bar`: `Selected Tab` in, `Selected Tab` +
`Selected Tab Changed` out. Also `Pagination` (`Current Page`), `Rating`,
`Multi Select/Dropdown` (`Selection` in, `Selected Items` + `Changed` out). This one pattern
accounts for most of that 84%. If your component holds a value the page might care about, publish the
value AND the signal that it moved — a parent that has to poll for it cannot use it.

### 3. The flag block — chrome and behaviour are chosen at the instance
`Show Label`, `Show Summary`, `Show Rows Per Page`, `Disabled`, `Required`, `Clickable`,
`Removable`, `Mounted`. Named `show*`, `is*`, `has*`, `enable*`. Two pages wanting the same
card with and without its footer is one component and one boolean, never two components.

### 4. The state machine is the component's brain
A `States` node, and three idioms:
- **Variant selector.** `Component Inputs.<enum port> → States.currentState`. 🔴 `currentState` is
  two ports sharing one name: a static string OUTPUT, and — once `states` is set — a generated enum
  INPUT. The input is the wire that switches a variant. Measured in `toast` (`Type`), `xano`
  (`Request Type`), `media-query` (`Debugger Position`). One `size` port driving a States node
  beats three components called Small, Medium and Large.
- **Boolean visual switch.** `Condition.ontrue/onfalse → States.to-<X>/to-<Y>`.
- **Operation lifecycle.** `File Upload` runs `Idle,Picking,Uploading,Done,Failed`; `Auth Pages`
  runs an Idle/Busy pair and drives the submit button's `enabled` from it.
⚠️ A chain of `Condition` nodes each setting one colour is this pattern written badly. One States
node, one input, every property it implies.
🔴 **A `Variable` is one value for the whole app**, by name, however many times the component is
placed. Keep an open flag, a selected tab, a pick or a draft in one, place the component twice, and
every copy opens, selects, picks and drafts together. It looks fine with one copy on the page, which
is why it ships. A component's own state is a `States` node, a `Component Object` (every instance
has its own), or a `Counter` or `Switch`. It lasts as long as that copy: hidden and shown again
(`mounted` off, then on) it keeps its value, and so does a `For Each` row whose id is still in the
new list. A `For Each` Refresh, a row that leaves the list and comes back, and a page left and
returned to each build a NEW copy that starts empty; tick the page's `Keep When Leaving` to keep
the page. When every copy really should share the value, like a row of filter pills writing one
filter, write "shared on purpose" in that node's comment: the validator warns about a Variable in a
component drawn twice until it says so.

### 5. A component can be a parameter
`Multi Select/Dropdown` exposes `Option Template` and `Pill Template` and wires them straight
into `For Each.template`. The consumer supplies the component that draws the row, so the container
is written once and never again.

### 6. Polymorphic rows
`For Each.templateType: "dynamic"` plus a `templateScript` that picks the component per row from
the row's own data — `Table/Row` (`component = '../' + item.Type + ' Cell'`), `Show Toast`,
`Filters`, `Form`. A heterogeneous list is one repeater, not a hand-built branch per type.

### 7. The slot
`Component Children` marks where the consumer's children land: `Page Header`,
`Table/Base Cell`, and in production apps every modal, context menu and collapsible group. A
container that can only hold what it was built to hold is not a container. ⚠️ A slot is not an
excuse to skip the rest: `Page Header` still takes `Title`, `Subtitle` and
`Breadcrumbs` and still publishes `Crumb Clicked` and `Crumb Target`, and `Table/Row`
— which draws nothing of its own — publishes `Click`, because a row nobody can click on is a
picture of a table.

### 8. Failure is a port
`Success` / `Failure` on every cloud action component; `Error`, `Failed` and `State` on
`File Upload`; `Has Error` on `Form Fields/Labelled Select`. **Fifty-five** components in the
shipped library publish one of these. If your component can fail, its failure is an output, not a
console message — the page cannot show what it is never told.

### 9. Data-shaped inputs
One array port feeding a `For Each`: `Items`, `Options`, `Headers`, `Filters`,
`Rows Per Page Options`. Never one port per row, and never a component per row.
Two lists may number their plain rows the same (`l0`, `l1`…): each list keeps its own rows. An id still
names one record for the whole app, though, so anything that finds a row *by its id* (an `Object` node
given the row's `Id`, a page writing to `itemActionItemId`) finds the first list's row. Inside a row,
read it with an `Object` node set to `From repeater`; give rows the page edits by id ids no other
list uses.

### 10. The named utility publishes too
`Component Inputs` → one or two working nodes → `Component Outputs`, under a name that is a job:
`Format full name`, `Is Trainer check`, `Sanitise email` — never `Function 3`, never
`Helper`. A logic component with no `Component Outputs` is a node with extra steps, because the
parent cannot read the result. Put it in a shared logic folder, not beside the page that happened to
need it first: findability is the case for extracting it and reuse is the bonus. **However small** is
meant literally — 48 of the 83 logic-only components in the shipped library are one or two working
nodes, and a production app's shared folder holds 17 of them instantiated 50 times, `Format full
name` alone nine times.

### A repeated row publishes to the repeater, not to nowhere
Rows end up mute because it looks as if there is nowhere to wire them: the page never places the
row, a `For Each` does. The repeater publishes for you. Every output port on the template
component reappears on the repeater itself — a `signal` as `itemOutputSignal-<name>`, a value as
`itemOutput-<name>` — beside `itemActionItemId`, the id of the row that raised it. Take the
trigger and the id from that same node and the write lands on exactly the row that was clicked.

🔴 **The id only moves if the signal is consumed.** A repeater tracks an item output only when
something is connected to it, so an `itemActionItemId` wire with no `itemOutputSignal-…` wire
beside it reads empty forever, and the delete that looked wired never fires.

THE TRAPS — read these before anything else. Each one fails SILENTLY.

1. A component's interface is a `Component Inputs` node, and its ports must be plugged "output".
   That inversion is real: values flow OUT of that node into the graph, so "output" is what makes
   them component INPUTS. Plugged "input" the port joins no interface and every wire drawn from it
   is dropped. A component with no interface renders identically however many times you place it.
2. An instance parameter that names no input is discarded without a word. A component instance has
   ONLY the ports its Component Inputs declares — no layout, style or lifecycle ports of its own.
   Set the parameters on the instance; declare the matching inputs on the component.
3. Inline row data is a `Static Data` node: a JSON array in one parameter, fed to a `For Each`.
   Nobody finds this node. Reach for it before hand-writing three copies of a card.
4. `Columns` is the only node in the runtime that reflows. Its layout string is integers and
   spaces — "1 1 2", never "1fr 1fr". Its autoFit mode needs no layout string at all. A Group with
   flexWrap cannot collapse on a narrow screen, because no Group anywhere has a breakpoint.
5. An absolute-positioned Group with no width or height fills its parent: dimensions default to
   100%. That is the badge pill that renders as a page-sized block.
6. Colour and spacing take design tokens — "var(--space-4)", never "#3b82f6" or a bare pixel count.
   Call get_style_vocabulary for what this project actually has.
7. Verify by looking. Call `render_report` when you have written anything visual: it renders the
   project headless and returns the numbers and the screenshots. A graph is a claim; a render is
   evidence. An image URL that returns 200 can still be a picture of the wrong thing.
8. NODES BEFORE CODE, AND NEVER ALTERNATE BETWEEN THEM.

   step — `Substring`, `String Format`, `String Mapper`, `Condition`, `Counter`,
   `Number Remapper` — place that node rather than writing the same thing into an Expression or a
   Function. It reads off the canvas, and the user can change it without opening a code editor.

   all, do ALL of it inside that ONE code node. Never split one calculation into a code node, then
   a library node, then more code — `JavaScriptFunction` → `Substring` → `JavaScriptFunction`
   is worse than either the single Function or the plain chain of nodes it replaced.
   Decide it per calculation: covered by one library node ⇒ use the node; needs code at all ⇒ one
   code node, all of it.
9. THREE WAYS TO COMPUTE, and reaching past them costs the user a node that cannot run.
   - `Expression` — One line of maths or logic over a few inputs. Every name you use in the line becomes an input port. No signal — it recalculates whenever an input changes.

   wherever either would do — split, slice, replace, includes. Keep bodies short enough to read
   in one go. Write `Outputs.X = value` for a value and `Outputs.X()` for a signal; a value

## Components are the unit of good work

**The order comes first.** Settle the look and the screen list before you decide what the components
are — the design doctrine's §"The order" says how, and it is not optional sequencing advice. A
component tree is a decomposition of a list of screens, so a tree decided before that list exists is
a guess; and a look decided after the components is a repaint of every one of them, which is a thing
nobody ever actually does.

Factoring is the default. A page assembled from named section components is easier to read, review
and change than the same page as one long column of nodes.

- **A named section is a component.** Hero, nav, card, form, footer, filter bar. If you would name it
  out loud, it gets its own component and the page instantiates it.
- **Repetition is data.** Two or more structurally identical siblings become one component driven by
  a Repeater over a data source. Never duplicate a subtree by hand.
- **Logic clusters are components.** Three or more logic nodes cooperating on one job get their own
  component with a declared interface, rather than sitting beside the visual nodes.
- **Shared or long code is a script file.** Code two Functions need, or a Function body long enough
  that you would change one line of it, goes in `scripts/<name>.js` (`write_script_file`), listed
  under the Function's `uses` and called as `Scripts.<name>`. `edit_script_file` then changes one
  line without sending the file again; a Function's own code can only be replaced whole.
- **Interfaces are deliberate.** Component Inputs/Outputs carry what varies per instance. Shared app
  state goes through Variables and Objects, not through prop drilling. A component's own state never
  does: a Variable is one value however many times the component is placed, so two copies share it.
- **Placement.** Used once, next to its page. Used twice or plausibly reusable, in a shared folder.
- **Say why on the node.** A node's `label` says what it is for; its `comment` says why it is the way
  it is. Write one where the next reader would otherwise change something and break it — a decision that
  had an alternative, a rule from outside the app that the graph cannot state, or a trap. Omit it when
  the type and label already say it: a comment restating either is noise, and most nodes need none.
- **A named utility is a component however small it is.** A Function that turns a name into
  "A. Surname", a permission check, a date format, a string the API wants in a shape nobody
  remembers — if a builder on another page would rewrite it rather than find it, give it a name and
  a folder. This is the most reused thing in real Noodl codebases and it is usually ONE working
  node: LearnBook's shared logic folders hold 37 such components instantiated 107 times, with
  `Format full name`, `Is Trainer check` and `Generate Google icon object` at nine uses each; 45 of
  the 80 logic-only components the original team shipped in `library/prefabs` are one or two working
  nodes. Findability is the case and reuse is the bonus — a named `Sanitise email` in a shared
  folder is the second builder's answer, an anonymous Function on page 4 is not.

**When not to.** An unnamed wrapper, or a two-node group used once and doing nothing you would say
out loud, is not a component — it is a file and a hop that bought nothing. A page with one section
has one section. ⚠️ **Size is not the test, and a small graph is not the exception.** The test is
whether the thing has a name a person would use; if it does, extract it at one node, and if it does
not, three nodes will not save it.

**Rule of thumb.** A component graph past ~25 nodes is telling you it wanted to be several.

You know what becomes a component. This is the other half — what its interface carries — and it is

any `Component Outputs`. Across the components the original Noodl team shipped in the prefab
library, **84%** do. That gap is the whole difference between a part and a display sink: a sink takes
text, draws it in one fixed place, and tells nobody anything, so every wire it should have owned ends
up back on the page around it — including a wrapper `Group` whose only job is to push it into
position.

Expose your own box: `Align X`, `Align Y`, `Margin Top/Right/Bottom/Left`, `Position`,
`Width`, `Mounted`. Almost every prefab exposes exactly this block — `Toggle Switch`,
`Date Picker`, `Tab Bar`, `Pagination`, `Rating`. Skip it and the parent wraps every instance
in a single-child `Group` that exists for nothing but spacing, which is a node the page keeps
forever and a decision the component should have owned.

`Toggle Switch` takes `State` and publishes `State` and `State Changed`. `Date Picker`:

`Selected Tab Changed` out. Also `Pagination` (`Current Page`), `Rating`,

card with and without its footer is one component and one boolean, never two components.

A `States` node, and three idioms:

`Multi Select/Dropdown` exposes `Option Template` and `Pill Template` and wires them straight

   write, and it arrives with an interface the original Noodl team designed — ports, outputs and a
   state machine — which is a better starting point than a leaf authored from nothing.

Only then author them.

4. **And when you have built something good, put it back.** `export_to_library({component, slug,
   label, description})` takes a component out of this project and writes it to the shelf as an
   installable entry — carrying the components it places, the styles and variants it uses, its
   assets and any code module its nodes come from, so it renders in a project that has never seen
   it. Design tokens travel by NAME, which is what makes an installed part wear the new project's
   look instead of dragging this one's palette along. A part worth exporting is one you would reach
   for again: a named utility, a section you got right, a control with a real interface.

**Why this is an order and not just two more rules.** A look decided after the components is a
repaint of every one of them, so it never actually happens: each component is already correct on its
own terms, nobody wants to reopen it, and the app ships wearing whatever the first leaf authored
happened to choose. The same is true of a screen list — a component tree invented before anyone said
what the screens are is a guess that later screens have to be bent around.

**Why the shelf is a step and not a footnote.** The library and the authoring path ship in the same
server, and until CMP-004 nothing in the briefing mentioned it — so every part of every app was
built from scratch beside a shelf of parts. Checking is one cheap call before the work; not checking
costs the whole part, and costs it again on the next app. This is the same bargain as reaching for a
CSS framework instead of writing the styles: you are not saving typing, you are inheriting decisions
somebody already got right.

**And why step 4 is what makes step 3 worth anything.** A shelf that is only ever read is a fixed
set of parts that ages. A shelf that is also written to is a library that gets better every time
anybody builds anything — which is the difference between every app inheriting the best component
anyone has built and every app starting from nothing.

**What "settled" means, stated so a person can check it:** somebody can open the project and read
back the accent, the surface ramp and the page list before a single component has been authored. If
they cannot, it is not settled — it is being decided one leaf at a time, which is the failure this
section exists to stop.

7:### 4. Colour: one accent, spent carefully
8:
9:Six roles carry a whole page: `--background`, `--surface`, `--foreground`, `--muted-foreground`,
10:`--border`, and ONE `--primary`. The accent appears on at most three kinds of thing (say: primary
11:button, eyebrow, price) — an accent on everything is an accent on nothing. Emit
12:`var(--token)` always; a raw hex in a parameter is a bug, not a shortcut.
13:
14:**Contrast is two rules, not one.** Text needs 4.5:1 against what is behind it. A **control's**
15:border — an input, an outline button — is the only thing telling the user where that control is, so
16:it needs 3:1; a decorative card hairline is exempt and should stay subtle. One border token cannot
17:be both: keep `--border` for hairlines and a distinct `--border-control` at 3:1 for controls.
18:Trying to make one token do both is how a real project ended up with 143 controls at 1.00:1.
19:
20:**Every band on a landing page does not get the same ground.** A page where no section ever changes
21:what is behind it is the WordPress-starter tell, whatever the type does. `Group` has four ways to
22:carry a ground and you should use at least three of them on a marketing page:
23:
24:- `backgroundColor` — a flat fill. `var(--background)` and `var(--surface)` alternating.
25:- `backgroundGradient` — a gradient token: `var(--gradient-brand)` (the brand wash),
26:  `var(--gradient-deep)` (ink into brand), `var(--gradient-spotlight)` (an off-centre glow),
27:  `var(--gradient-surface)` (a quiet mid-page wash). Put `var(--primary-foreground)` text on the
28:  first three; they are dark.
29:- `backgroundImage` — a picture as the ground, with `backgroundSize: "cover"`.
30:- **Both together.** `backgroundGradient` paints ON TOP of `backgroundImage`, so
31:  `var(--gradient-scrim)` over a photograph is what keeps a headline readable on a picture you
32:  have not seen. This is one node — never an `Image` with an absolutely-positioned `Group` over it.
33:
34:**Depth is an alpha fill, not `opacity`.** `opacity` on a `Group` fades its own children, so a
35:see-through panel comes from `backgroundColor: "var(--surface-glass)"` with
36:`borderColor: "var(--border-glass)"` and `backdropBlur` — the `glassPanel` composition. It reads
37:only on a dark ground. `boxShadowEnabled` with a `--shadow-*` token lifts a card off its surface;
38:`position: "absolute"` with `zIndex` overlaps two things deliberately. All of these are ordinary
39:ports on `Group` — the absence a flat page is showing is never the engine's.

41:### 5. Images and icons are not decoration
42:
43:A visual page with no `Image` and no `Icon` cannot look designed, and no amount of spacing will
44:rescue it. Every listing gets a picture, every feature row gets an icon.
45:
46:**Every project created here already has both, offline.** You do not need a URL and you must not
47:invent one:
48:
49:- `noodl_modules/starter-imagery/` — **44 real photographs**, CC0, already cropped for the job they
50:  are for. Reference one as `"noodl_modules/starter-imagery/work-welder.webp"`. 🔴 **Get the list
51:  from `get_style_vocabulary`'s `imagery` block and pick by SUBJECT**, not by guessing a filename:
52:  `hero` (16:9 band grounds, chosen dark enough to carry display type), `work` (somebody making
53:  something), `people`, `food`, `animals`, `texture` (surfaces) and `avatar` (256px squares
54:  framed on a face — there are six DIFFERENT faces, and a testimonial row wearing one face three
55:  times is the thing a reader notices before they read a word).
56:  **A picture has to say something about the subject.** A page whose every image is the same
57:  abstract is decorated, not designed — that page exists, it is the VIB-004 marketing demo, and
58:  "the pictures communicate nothing" is precisely why it is not finished.
59:- The same directory also holds six abstract SVGs (`ground-aurora.svg`, `ground-ridge.svg`,
60:  `tile-1/2/3.svg`, `portrait.svg`). They are the fallback for when **no photograph would be
61:  honest** about the subject — an app about accountancy is not improved by a stock welder. 🔴 Never
62:  use a `ground-*` as a SUBJECT picture: they are designed to be dark and empty so text reads on
63:  them, and `ui-split-hero` pointed its media column at `ground-ridge.svg` and rendered a black
64:  rectangle at the top of the most-copied recipe in the corpus.
65:- `noodl_modules/lucide-icons/` — the glyph set. 🔴 **Get the value from
66:  `get_style_vocabulary`'s `icons` block and copy it whole.** An icon parameter is
67:  `{"class": "lucide", "code": "icon-check", "codeAsClass": true}`, and all three fields matter:
68:  `class` and `codeAsClass` come from the installed set's manifest, not from the glyph name, and
69:  a value **missing `codeAsClass` renders the glyph's NAME as visible text**. The curated list is
70:  a starting point rather than a ceiling — the bundled font carries all 1998 Lucide glyphs and the
71:  stylesheet has a rule for every one, so any name from lucide.dev works with `icon-` in front of
72:  it.
73:
74:- Give the image a real box: `sizeMode: "explicit"`, a `width`, a `height`, `objectFit: "cover"`.
75:- Put it in a `clip: true` parent so the card's radius actually cuts the picture.
76:- **An external URL is an unchecked claim.** A URL that 404s, or a photo of the wrong thing, undoes
77:  every other decision on the page. If you have not seen it, use the starter imagery instead.
78:
79:### 6. Reuse recipes, do not re-decide
80:
81:🔴 **A band and a shell are one thing, not two.** Every full-width section is a `band` (or
82:`bandSurface`) holding exactly ONE `shell` — `maxWidth: 1200px` with `var(--space-6)` either
83:side — and everything else goes inside the shell. A band whose content is not in a shell runs edge
84:to edge, and it is worse when the bands below it are inset: the reader sees three sections agree
85:about the margin and one disagree, which reads as a bug rather than as a choice. **The gutter is
86:the same on every band of a page or it is a mistake.**
87:
88:Before authoring, fix a handful of named parameter sets and reuse them verbatim: a `card`, a
89:`shell`, a `sectionHead`, one `primaryButton`, one `outlineButton`, and a type ramp. A page whose
90:cards disagree about their own radius reads as careless even when each card is defensible. Where a
91:variant exists in the style vocabulary, copy its concrete parameters — `variant` and `size` are
92:connection-only ports and setting them as parameters is discarded AND rejected.
93:
94:### 7. Responsive: `Columns` is the only thing that reflows
95:
96:**A `Group` never responds to width. There are no media queries and no breakpoints anywhere in the
97:runtime except on one node.** A row of Groups is frozen at whatever proportions you authored, so a
98:two-column hero stays two columns at 390px and a 32%-wide card becomes 120px wide. Everything on a
99:page that is arranged in more than one column must therefore be a `net.noodl.visual.columns` node.
100:
101:- **Grid of unknown length** (products, posts, tiles): `sizing: "autoFit"` with a `minWidth` of
102:  260–320px. No breakpoints to maintain — it fits as many columns as will hold that width and
103:  reflows on its own. This is the right default for anything fed by a Repeater.
104:- **A fixed arrangement** (a 2-up hero, a 3-up feature strip, a 4-up footer): `layoutString`
105:  (`"1 1"`, `"1 1 1"`, `"2 1"` for an uneven split), plus `mediumBreakpoint`/`mediumLayout` and
106:  `smallBreakpoint`/`smallLayout` to collapse it — typically `"1"` under about 700px.
107:- Breakpoints are measured against the **container**, not the viewport, so the same component
108:  behaves correctly inside a sidebar, a modal or a repeater cell.
109:- A `Columns` node handles a Repeater child correctly: the Repeater itself is not a layout
110:  participant, and its items each get a column box.
111:- Use `marginX` for the gutter between `Columns` tracks; a percentage gap on a wrapped Group is a
112:  desktop-only trick and stops being one the moment the layout must collapse.
113:
114:**Type scales through the token, not the port.** `fontSize` still has no responsive form — but
115:`--display-sm`/`--display-md`/`--display-lg` are `clamp()` values, so one parameter gives you
116:44px at 390px and 96px at 1900px with no breakpoint anywhere. Use them for the display headline and
117:for any heading over a picture. The fixed `--text-*` sizes stay fixed and stay right for body,
118:labels and section headings, where scaling with the window is wrong.
119:
120:Check the narrow width before saying it is done: nothing should exceed the viewport
121:(`el.getBoundingClientRect().width > window.innerWidth`), and a multi-column band should have
122:become one column.
123:
124:### 8. The mechanics that silently undo layout
125:
126:Each of these was found by measuring a rendered DOM, and none is visible in a graph:
127:
128:- **A wrapped flex row does not shrink its children; an unwrapped one does.** This is why a row of
129:  Groups appears to work and a wrapped grid of them does not: without wrapping, children shrink to
130:  share the width; with it, each item keeps whatever width it was given. If you must use a wrapped
131:  Group at all, every item needs an explicit percentage track width AND a percentage gap
132:  (`width: 32%` with `columnGap: 2%`). **Prefer `Columns` — see §7 — because a wrapped Group
133:  cannot collapse at any width.**
134:- **`sizeMode` gates other ports.** On `Image`, `net.noodl.controls.button` and `textinput`,
135:  `width`/`height`/`objectFit` are INERT unless `sizeMode: "explicit"`. A `width: 100%` input that
136:  renders 170px wide is this, every time.
137:- **A dimension is `{ value, unit }`.** `width`, `height`, `maxWidth`, `minWidth` default to `%`,
138:  so a bare `width: 228` renders at 228%. Units-typed numbers (padding, gap, radius, fontSize)
139:  accept `{value, unit}` or a `var(--token)` string.
140:- **Falsiness is free conditional rendering.** Wire a record field straight into a Group's
141:  `visible` port: an empty `badge` string and a `compareAtPrice` of `0` then hide their own chrome
142:  with no logic node. Without it, every row carries an empty pill.
143:- **`Text` is not a box.** It has no background, padding, border or `textDecoration`. Wrap it in a
144:  `Group` for the box; use `styleCss` for the rare CSS property no port covers (strikethrough).
145:- Use the gap ports (`rowGap`, `columnGap`) for spacing between siblings, never margins on the
146:  children — margins do not collapse the way a designer expects and leave the last item uneven.
147:
148:### 9. Design the empty and the loading state
149:
150:A list with no rows should say what it is and what to do, not render nothing. An empty state is a
151:small designed object: icon, one line of explanation, one action.
152:
153:### 10. Words are part of the visual design
154:
155:Placeholder copy makes a competent layout look like a template. Write the real thing: specific,
156:concrete, and in the product's own voice — "Between 20 and 60 of a thing, then we move on" rather
157:than "High quality products". Numbers, materials and constraints read as designed; adjectives do
158:not. Never ship "Lorem ipsum", "Welcome to our store", or "Card title".
159:
160:### 11. You have not finished until you have looked at it
161:
162:A graph is a claim; a render is evidence. Render the project, screenshot it, and measure the DOM
163:before saying it is done. Three checks catch most of what goes wrong:
164:
165:1. `document.documentElement.scrollWidth > clientWidth` — something is overflowing.
166:2. The set of `getComputedStyle(el).fontWeight` across text nodes — if it is `{"400"}`, there is no
167:   hierarchy on the page.
168:3. The `offsetWidth` of the items in a grid — if they all equal the container, the grid is a column.
169:===== backendDoctrine
170:## The backend in one sentence
171:
172:A workflow orchestrates; a cloud function computes; a workflow calls cloud functions.
173:
174:## The runtime is the path
175:
176:A component under `#__cloud__/` runs in the cloud runtime; everything else runs in the browser.
177:The two share no node set: browser nodes (Text, Group, Page…) do not exist in the cloud runtime and
178:cloud nodes (`noodl.cloud.request`, `noodl.cloud.secret`…) do not exist in the browser — the
179:write gate rejects a node in the wrong runtime (`wrong-runtime-node`), and a component instance
180:may only be placed inside a component of the same runtime.
181:
182:## Function vs helper — two kinds of cloud component
183:
184:- A cloud **function** is a cloud component whose graph holds a `noodl.cloud.request` node:
185:  Request in → logic → Response out. It is callable as `POST /functions/<name>` and from the
186:  app's Cloud Function node. **Its interface is the `params` on the Request node** (a
187:  comma-separated list of names, each becoming an output port) — NOT a Component Inputs node.
188:  Answer on every path with a `noodl.cloud.response`; a path that ends without one hangs the
189:  request until the timeout.
190:- A cloud **helper** is a cloud component with no Request node. It is not an endpoint — calling it
191:  by name 404s, and it never appears in the permissions panel. It is the unit of reuse: instantiate
192:  it from other cloud graphs (its interface IS Component Inputs/Outputs, like any component), or
193:  hand it to Run Tasks as the per-item template.
194:
195:## Compose the backend the way you compose pages
196:
197:The shipped prefab idiom, and the one to copy: thin function shells that receive the request and
198:delegate to shared helpers; one Settings helper wrapping `noodl.cloud.secret` so a credential is
199:read in exactly one place; nested names (`Stripe/Subscriptions/Cancel`) to group a family.
200:Secrets live in the backend's `functions` namespace — the only one a graph can read — and do not
201:travel with a deploy; provision them per environment.
202:
203:## Auth at the boundary
204:
205:The Request node's `Allow Unauthenticated` is the function's default rule; a per-function
206:`call` rule set in the Permissions panel overrides it. Two consequences worth wiring for:
207:a workflow step calls its function IN PROCESS with no session, so a step-called function needs
208:`Allow Unauthenticated` ticked (the panel rule cannot fix a failing step); and a function holding
209:the system user/role nodes (`noodl.cloud.createuser`, `noodl.cloud.addusertorole`…) with no
210:call rule falls back to that checkbox — which, ticked, is account creation for the open internet.
211:
212:🔴 **The checkbox has two values and a real endpoint needs three, and there is no defaults
213:tier to make up the difference.** An undeclared COLLECTION falls back to
214:`defaults.permissions` and fails shut; an undeclared FUNCTION falls back to this port and
215:nothing in the security file can lower it. Unticked gets you `authenticated`, which is
216:**any account that can sign up** — not an administrator. And a cloud function **runs as
217:system**, so this gate is the only boundary in front of a privileged write: there is nothing
218:behind it.
219:
220:So an endpoint only an admin should reach **cannot be closed from the graph**. Declare it:
221:
222:```json
223:{ "functions": { "publishPage": { "call": "role:admin" } } }
224:```
225:
226:For a project rather than one backend, that block belongs in the project's
227:`nodegx.security.json`, which provisioning installs as the backend's `security.json` on a
228:first start that has none.
229:
230:⚠️ A deploy beyond localhost now REFUSES to start while any endpoint resolves only from the
231:port, naming each one and printing the block to paste. A loopback backend does not, so this
232:is a rule to know while building rather than one the machine will remind you of.
233:
234:## Five things a deployed graph does not do the way the canvas does
235:
236:Every one of these was found by running an MCP-authored cloud function on a real backend, and every
237:one was green through both authoring doors first. They share a cause worth stating on its own: **a
238:deployed backend has no editor connection**, and a surprising amount of the runtime's helpfulness is
239:behind `isRunningLocally()`.
240:
241:**1. Declare a code node's custom signal outputs, or they are dead.** `Outputs.done()` is a call,
242:and it resolves only if `out-done` is on the node as a `signal` port. The editor derives those
243:ports by parsing the script and saves what it derived; the MCP door derives nothing. So an authored
244:`JavaScriptFunction` needs them written out —
245:`"ports": [{ "name": "out-ok", "plug": "output", "type": "signal" }]` beside the
246:`functionScript`. Undeclared, the script throws mid-run, no Response node is reached, and the
247:caller waits out the 30-second timeout. The built-in `success`/`failure` outcome outputs are
248:declared on the node type and always work — which is why this is invisible until you name your own
249:signal.
250:
251:**2. A signal is not a promise that the values beside it have arrived.** Values are queued per input
252:name and drained a pass at a time, so a node triggered by one producer's signal can run before
253:another producer's value reaches it. A code node fed by **two** producers must therefore guard:
254:`if (Inputs.items === undefined || Inputs.flag === undefined) return;`. Returning is safe and
255:cheap — `runOnValueChange` is ticked by default, so a late value re-runs the node by itself
256:(⚠️ unless you unticked it under rule 5, in which case the guard's job is to make an early run
257:harmless rather than to wait for a later one).
258:**Acting on the incomplete first run is what cannot be undone.** Better still, prefer a chain to a
259:fan-out, so every consumer's values are at least one hop older than its trigger. ⚠️ This is why
260:`receive` is not the universal answer: it fires once every parameter output on the **Request node**
261:has updated, and says nothing about when those values reach a node three hops away.
262:
263:**3. A `Query Records` node fetches once, unfiltered, when the graph is built.**
264:`collectionName` and `visualFilter` are parameters, and setting either schedules a fetch. That
265:first query has no `qp-` value, a rule with an undefined value is *dropped* rather than failed, and
266:a dropped rule is no `where` — every row in the class, delivered on `fetched` before your request
267:has done anything. For a query **with** a filter parameter, switch off the implicit triggers and
268:leave `Do` unwired, so the filter value arriving is the only trigger:
269:`"runOnChange-collectionName": false, "runOnChange-querySettings": false`.
270:
271:⚠️ **The precondition of that fix is a filter PORT, not a filter.** A query filtered by a
272:**literal** is already narrowed at graph-build time and has no parameter left to trigger it, so it
273:keeps the defaults. 🔴 **And whichever way you go, do not do both:** a query with the boxes **on**
274:*and* a wire into `storageFetch` runs everything downstream of it **twice** — one call to
275:`claimSite` wrote its `SiteSettings` singleton as two identical rows eleven milliseconds apart,
276:with no error anywhere and both readers taking `rows[0]`. Boxes on and `Do` unwired, or boxes off
277:and `Do` wired. The second is the shape for an unfiltered query whose reader must not decide
278:early, because it puts the fetch *after* whatever triggers it.
279:
280:**4. `points to` cannot narrow anything from a cloud function, and it widens instead of failing.**
281:It is the one operator that needs the collection schema, the schema cache is never populated in the
282:cloud runtime, and the translator's refusal is reported through the editor connection that is not
283:there. The query then runs with no filter at all. **Use a plain id String and `equal to` for a link
284:a cloud function has to filter on.** Pointers are fine to write and fine to read back; it is
285:filtering on one that does not work here.
286:
287:**5. Wiring `Run` does not stop a code node running on its own, and `isEmpty` cannot tell
288:"empty" from "not yet".** Harmless apart, a security defect together. `Run` is **purely
289:additive** — wiring it adds a trigger and unticks nothing, and every input is ticked by default —
290:so a gate wired `Query Records.fetched → Run` reads like "decides after the query" and does not:
291:it also re-runs as each input value arrives, and that run happens *before* the fetch. Meanwhile
292:`isEmpty` is `true` before the first query has run **and** `true` for a collection that
293:matched nothing: one value for opposite facts. In `claimSite` the pair read an already-claimed
294:site as unclaimed and put a second, unrelated caller into the `admin` role, while still answering
295:`This site cannot be claimed.` to the request that did it. Fix it twice: **untick the boxes**
296:(`"runOnChange-in-expected": false`) on a node that has a `Run` wire, so its trigger is really
297:its only trigger, and **guard on `items`** — `if (Inputs.rows === undefined) return;` — which is
298:the one output of a Query Records node that separates *matched nothing* (`[]`) from *has not run*
299:(`undefined`). ⚠️ Generalise the guard: `isEmpty`, `count` and `firstItemId` all answer
300:before there is anything to answer about.
301:
302:## Which one do I reach for?
303:
304:"Run this now and answer the user" → a cloud function, called from the app. "Every night / when a
305:record changes / retry three times then wait" → a workflow, calling cloud functions to do the work.
306:Real work — records, HTTP, mail, code — always lives in a cloud function, never in a workflow step.

31:  `var(--gradient-scrim)` over a photograph is what keeps a headline readable on a picture you
32:  have not seen. This is one node — never an `Image` with an absolutely-positioned `Group` over it.
33:
34:**Depth is an alpha fill, not `opacity`.** `opacity` on a `Group` fades its own children, so a
35:see-through panel comes from `backgroundColor: "var(--surface-glass)"` with
36:`borderColor: "var(--border-glass)"` and `backdropBlur` — the `glassPanel` composition. It reads
37:only on a dark ground. `boxShadowEnabled` with a `--shadow-*` token lifts a card off its surface;
38:`position: "absolute"` with `zIndex` overlaps two things deliberately. All of these are ordinary
39:ports on `Group` — the absence a flat page is showing is never the engine's.
40:
41:### 5. Images and icons are not decoration
42:
43:A visual page with no `Image` and no `Icon` cannot look designed, and no amount of spacing will
44:rescue it. Every listing gets a picture, every feature row gets an icon.
45:
46:**Every project created here already has both, offline.** You do not need a URL and you must not
47:invent one:
48:
49:- `noodl_modules/starter-imagery/` — **44 real photographs**, CC0, already cropped for the job they
50:  are for. Reference one as `"noodl_modules/starter-imagery/work-welder.webp"`. 🔴 **Get the list
51:  from `get_style_vocabulary`'s `imagery` block and pick by SUBJECT**, not by guessing a filename:
52:  `hero` (16:9 band grounds, chosen dark enough to carry display type), `work` (somebody making
53:  something), `people`, `food`, `animals`, `texture` (surfaces) and `avatar` (256px squares
54:  framed on a face — there are six DIFFERENT faces, and a testimonial row wearing one face three
55:  times is the thing a reader notices before they read a word).
56:  **A picture has to say something about the subject.** A page whose every image is the same
57:  abstract is decorated, not designed — that page exists, it is the VIB-004 marketing demo, and
58:  "the pictures communicate nothing" is precisely why it is not finished.
59:- The same directory also holds six abstract SVGs (`ground-aurora.svg`, `ground-ridge.svg`,
60:  `tile-1/2/3.svg`, `portrait.svg`). They are the fallback for when **no photograph would be
61:  honest** about the subject — an app about accountancy is not improved by a stock welder. 🔴 Never
62:  use a `ground-*` as a SUBJECT picture: they are designed to be dark and empty so text reads on
63:  them, and `ui-split-hero` pointed its media column at `ground-ridge.svg` and rendered a black
64:  rectangle at the top of the most-copied recipe in the corpus.
65:- `noodl_modules/lucide-icons/` — the glyph set. 🔴 **Get the value from
66:  `get_style_vocabulary`'s `icons` block and copy it whole.** An icon parameter is
67:  `{"class": "lucide", "code": "icon-check", "codeAsClass": true}`, and all three fields matter:
68:  `class` and `codeAsClass` come from the installed set's manifest, not from the glyph name, and
69:  a value **missing `codeAsClass` renders the glyph's NAME as visible text**. The curated list is
70:  a starting point rather than a ceiling — the bundled font carries all 1998 Lucide glyphs and the
71:  stylesheet has a rule for every one, so any name from lucide.dev works with `icon-` in front of
72:  it.
73:
74:- Give the image a real box: `sizeMode: "explicit"`, a `width`, a `height`, `objectFit: "cover"`.
75:- Put it in a `clip: true` parent so the card's radius actually cuts the picture.
76:- **An external URL is an unchecked claim.** A URL that 404s, or a photo of the wrong thing, undoes
77:  every other decision on the page. If you have not seen it, use the starter imagery instead.
78:
79:### 6. Reuse recipes, do not re-decide
80:
81:🔴 **A band and a shell are one thing, not two.** Every full-width section is a `band` (or
82:`bandSurface`) holding exactly ONE `shell` — `maxWidth: 1200px` with `var(--space-6)` either
83:side — and everything else goes inside the shell. A band whose content is not in a shell runs edge
84:to edge, and it is worse when the bands below it are inset: the reader sees three sections agree
85:about the margin and one disagree, which reads as a bug rather than as a choice. **The gutter is
86:the same on every band of a page or it is a mistake.**
87:
88:Before authoring, fix a handful of named parameter sets and reuse them verbatim: a `card`, a
89:`shell`, a `sectionHead`, one `primaryButton`, one `outlineButton`, and a type ramp. A page whose
90:cards disagree about their own radius reads as careless even when each card is defensible. Where a
91:variant exists in the style vocabulary, copy its concrete parameters — `variant` and `size` are
92:connection-only ports and setting them as parameters is discarded AND rejected.
93:
94:### 7. Responsive: `Columns` is the only thing that reflows
95:
96:**A `Group` never responds to width. There are no media queries and no breakpoints anywhere in the
97:runtime except on one node.** A row of Groups is frozen at whatever proportions you authored, so a
98:two-column hero stays two columns at 390px and a 32%-wide card becomes 120px wide. Everything on a
99:page that is arranged in more than one column must therefore be a `net.noodl.visual.columns` node.
100:
101:- **Grid of unknown length** (products, posts, tiles): `sizing: "autoFit"` with a `minWidth` of
102:  260–320px. No breakpoints to maintain — it fits as many columns as will hold that width and
103:  reflows on its own. This is the right default for anything fed by a Repeater.
104:- **A fixed arrangement** (a 2-up hero, a 3-up feature strip, a 4-up footer): `layoutString`
105:  (`"1 1"`, `"1 1 1"`, `"2 1"` for an uneven split), plus `mediumBreakpoint`/`mediumLayout` and
106:  `smallBreakpoint`/`smallLayout` to collapse it — typically `"1"` under about 700px.
107:- Breakpoints are measured against the **container**, not the viewport, so the same component
108:  behaves correctly inside a sidebar, a modal or a repeater cell.
109:- A `Columns` node handles a Repeater child correctly: the Repeater itself is not a layout
110:  participant, and its items each get a column box.
111:- Use `marginX` for the gutter between `Columns` tracks; a percentage gap on a wrapped Group is a
112:  desktop-only trick and stops being one the moment the layout must collapse.
113:
114:**Type scales through the token, not the port.** `fontSize` still has no responsive form — but
115:`--display-sm`/`--display-md`/`--display-lg` are `clamp()` values, so one parameter gives you
116:44px at 390px and 96px at 1900px with no breakpoint anywhere. Use them for the display headline and
117:for any heading over a picture. The fixed `--text-*` sizes stay fixed and stay right for body,
118:labels and section headings, where scaling with the window is wrong.
119:
120:Check the narrow width before saying it is done: nothing should exceed the viewport
121:(`el.getBoundingClientRect().width > window.innerWidth`), and a multi-column band should have
122:become one column.
123:
124:### 8. The mechanics that silently undo layout
125:
126:Each of these was found by measuring a rendered DOM, and none is visible in a graph:
127:
128:- **A wrapped flex row does not shrink its children; an unwrapped one does.** This is why a row of
129:  Groups appears to work and a wrapped grid of them does not: without wrapping, children shrink to
130:  share the width; with it, each item keeps whatever width it was given. If you must use a wrapped
131:  Group at all, every item needs an explicit percentage track width AND a percentage gap
132:  (`width: 32%` with `columnGap: 2%`). **Prefer `Columns` — see §7 — because a wrapped Group
133:  cannot collapse at any width.**
134:- **`sizeMode` gates other ports.** On `Image`, `net.noodl.controls.button` and `textinput`,
135:  `width`/`height`/`objectFit` are INERT unless `sizeMode: "explicit"`. A `width: 100%` input that
136:  renders 170px wide is this, every time.
137:- **A dimension is `{ value, unit }`.** `width`, `height`, `maxWidth`, `minWidth` default to `%`,
138:  so a bare `width: 228` renders at 228%. Units-typed numbers (padding, gap, radius, fontSize)
139:  accept `{value, unit}` or a `var(--token)` string.
140:- **Falsiness is free conditional rendering.** Wire a record field straight into a Group's
141:  `visible` port: an empty `badge` string and a `compareAtPrice` of `0` then hide their own chrome
142:  with no logic node. Without it, every row carries an empty pill.
143:- **`Text` is not a box.** It has no background, padding, border or `textDecoration`. Wrap it in a
144:  `Group` for the box; use `styleCss` for the rare CSS property no port covers (strikethrough).
145:- Use the gap ports (`rowGap`, `columnGap`) for spacing between siblings, never margins on the
146:  children — margins do not collapse the way a designer expects and leave the last item uneven.
147:
148:### 9. Design the empty and the loading state
149:
150:A list with no rows should say what it is and what to do, not render nothing. An empty state is a
151:small designed object: icon, one line of explanation, one action.
152:
153:### 10. Words are part of the visual design
154:
155:Placeholder copy makes a competent layout look like a template. Write the real thing: specific,
156:concrete, and in the product's own voice — "Between 20 and 60 of a thing, then we move on" rather
157:than "High quality products". Numbers, materials and constraints read as designed; adjectives do
158:not. Never ship "Lorem ipsum", "Welcome to our store", or "Card title".
159:
160:### 11. You have not finished until you have looked at it
161:
162:A graph is a claim; a render is evidence. Render the project, screenshot it, and measure the DOM
163:before saying it is done. Three checks catch most of what goes wrong:
164:
165:1. `document.documentElement.scrollWidth > clientWidth` — something is overflowing.
166:2. The set of `getComputedStyle(el).fontWeight` across text nodes — if it is `{"400"}`, there is no
167:   hierarchy on the page.
168:3. The `offsetWidth` of the items in a grid — if they all equal the container, the grid is a column.
169:===== backendDoctrine
170:## The backend in one sentence
171:
172:A workflow orchestrates; a cloud function computes; a workflow calls cloud functions.
173:
174:## The runtime is the path
175:
176:A component under `#__cloud__/` runs in the cloud runtime; everything else runs in the browser.
177:The two share no node set: browser nodes (Text, Group, Page…) do not exist in the cloud runtime and
178:cloud nodes (`noodl.cloud.request`, `noodl.cloud.secret`…) do not exist in the browser — the
179:write gate rejects a node in the wrong runtime (`wrong-runtime-node`), and a component instance
180:may only be placed inside a component of the same runtime.
181:
182:## Function vs helper — two kinds of cloud component
183:
184:- A cloud **function** is a cloud component whose graph holds a `noodl.cloud.request` node:
185:  Request in → logic → Response out. It is callable as `POST /functions/<name>` and from the
186:  app's Cloud Function node. **Its interface is the `params` on the Request node** (a
187:  comma-separated list of names, each becoming an output port) — NOT a Component Inputs node.
188:  Answer on every path with a `noodl.cloud.response`; a path that ends without one hangs the
189:  request until the timeout.
190:- A cloud **helper** is a cloud component with no Request node. It is not an endpoint — calling it
191:  by name 404s, and it never appears in the permissions panel. It is the unit of reuse: instantiate
192:  it from other cloud graphs (its interface IS Component Inputs/Outputs, like any component), or
193:  hand it to Run Tasks as the per-item template.
194:
195:## Compose the backend the way you compose pages
196:
197:The shipped prefab idiom, and the one to copy: thin function shells that receive the request and
198:delegate to shared helpers; one Settings helper wrapping `noodl.cloud.secret` so a credential is
199:read in exactly one place; nested names (`Stripe/Subscriptions/Cancel`) to group a family.
200:Secrets live in the backend's `functions` namespace — the only one a graph can read — and do not
201:travel with a deploy; provision them per environment.
202:
203:## Auth at the boundary
204:
205:The Request node's `Allow Unauthenticated` is the function's default rule; a per-function
206:`call` rule set in the Permissions panel overrides it. Two consequences worth wiring for:
207:a workflow step calls its function IN PROCESS with no session, so a step-called function needs
208:`Allow Unauthenticated` ticked (the panel rule cannot fix a failing step); and a function holding
209:the system user/role nodes (`noodl.cloud.createuser`, `noodl.cloud.addusertorole`…) with no
210:call rule falls back to that checkbox — which, ticked, is account creation for the open internet.
211:
212:🔴 **The checkbox has two values and a real endpoint needs three, and there is no defaults
213:tier to make up the difference.** An undeclared COLLECTION falls back to
214:`defaults.permissions` and fails shut; an undeclared FUNCTION falls back to this port and
215:nothing in the security file can lower it. Unticked gets you `authenticated`, which is
216:**any account that can sign up** — not an administrator. And a cloud function **runs as
217:system**, so this gate is the only boundary in front of a privileged write: there is nothing
218:behind it.
219:
220:So an endpoint only an admin should reach **cannot be closed from the graph**. Declare it:
221:
222:```json
223:{ "functions": { "publishPage": { "call": "role:admin" } } }
224:```
225:
226:For a project rather than one backend, that block belongs in the project's
227:`nodegx.security.json`, which provisioning installs as the backend's `security.json` on a
228:first start that has none.
229:
230:⚠️ A deploy beyond localhost now REFUSES to start while any endpoint resolves only from the
231:port, naming each one and printing the block to paste. A loopback backend does not, so this
232:is a rule to know while building rather than one the machine will remind you of.
233:
234:## Five things a deployed graph does not do the way the canvas does
235:
236:Every one of these was found by running an MCP-authored cloud function on a real backend, and every
237:one was green through both authoring doors first. They share a cause worth stating on its own: **a
238:deployed backend has no editor connection**, and a surprising amount of the runtime's helpfulness is
239:behind `isRunningLocally()`.
240:
241:**1. Declare a code node's custom signal outputs, or they are dead.** `Outputs.done()` is a call,
242:and it resolves only if `out-done` is on the node as a `signal` port. The editor derives those
243:ports by parsing the script and saves what it derived; the MCP door derives nothing. So an authored
244:`JavaScriptFunction` needs them written out —
245:`"ports": [{ "name": "out-ok", "plug": "output", "type": "signal" }]` beside the
246:`functionScript`. Undeclared, the script throws mid-run, no Response node is reached, and the
247:caller waits out the 30-second timeout. The built-in `success`/`failure` outcome outputs are
248:declared on the node type and always work — which is why this is invisible until you name your own
249:signal.
250:
251:**2. A signal is not a promise that the values beside it have arrived.** Values are queued per input
252:name and drained a pass at a time, so a node triggered by one producer's signal can run before
253:another producer's value reaches it. A code node fed by **two** producers must therefore guard:
254:`if (Inputs.items === undefined || Inputs.flag === undefined) return;`. Returning is safe and
255:cheap — `runOnValueChange` is ticked by default, so a late value re-runs the node by itself
256:(⚠️ unless you unticked it under rule 5, in which case the guard's job is to make an early run
257:harmless rather than to wait for a later one).
258:**Acting on the incomplete first run is what cannot be undone.** Better still, prefer a chain to a
259:fan-out, so every consumer's values are at least one hop older than its trigger. ⚠️ This is why
260:`receive` is not the universal answer: it fires once every parameter output on the **Request node**
261:has updated, and says nothing about when those values reach a node three hops away.
262:
263:**3. A `Query Records` node fetches once, unfiltered, when the graph is built.**
264:`collectionName` and `visualFilter` are parameters, and setting either schedules a fetch. That
265:first query has no `qp-` value, a rule with an undefined value is *dropped* rather than failed, and
266:a dropped rule is no `where` — every row in the class, delivered on `fetched` before your request
267:has done anything. For a query **with** a filter parameter, switch off the implicit triggers and
268:leave `Do` unwired, so the filter value arriving is the only trigger:
269:`"runOnChange-collectionName": false, "runOnChange-querySettings": false`.
270:
271:⚠️ **The precondition of that fix is a filter PORT, not a filter.** A query filtered by a
272:**literal** is already narrowed at graph-build time and has no parameter left to trigger it, so it
273:keeps the defaults. 🔴 **And whichever way you go, do not do both:** a query with the boxes **on**
274:*and* a wire into `storageFetch` runs everything downstream of it **twice** — one call to
275:`claimSite` wrote its `SiteSettings` singleton as two identical rows eleven milliseconds apart,
276:with no error anywhere and both readers taking `rows[0]`. Boxes on and `Do` unwired, or boxes off
277:and `Do` wired. The second is the shape for an unfiltered query whose reader must not decide
278:early, because it puts the fetch *after* whatever triggers it.
279:
280:**4. `points to` cannot narrow anything from a cloud function, and it widens instead of failing.**
281:It is the one operator that needs the collection schema, the schema cache is never populated in the
282:cloud runtime, and the translator's refusal is reported through the editor connection that is not
283:there. The query then runs with no filter at all. **Use a plain id String and `equal to` for a link
284:a cloud function has to filter on.** Pointers are fine to write and fine to read back; it is
285:filtering on one that does not work here.
286:
287:**5. Wiring `Run` does not stop a code node running on its own, and `isEmpty` cannot tell
288:"empty" from "not yet".** Harmless apart, a security defect together. `Run` is **purely
289:additive** — wiring it adds a trigger and unticks nothing, and every input is ticked by default —
290:so a gate wired `Query Records.fetched → Run` reads like "decides after the query" and does not:
291:it also re-runs as each input value arrives, and that run happens *before* the fetch. Meanwhile
292:`isEmpty` is `true` before the first query has run **and** `true` for a collection that
293:matched nothing: one value for opposite facts. In `claimSite` the pair read an already-claimed
294:site as unclaimed and put a second, unrelated caller into the `admin` role, while still answering
295:`This site cannot be claimed.` to the request that did it. Fix it twice: **untick the boxes**
296:(`"runOnChange-in-expected": false`) on a node that has a `Run` wire, so its trigger is really
297:its only trigger, and **guard on `items`** — `if (Inputs.rows === undefined) return;` — which is
298:the one output of a Query Records node that separates *matched nothing* (`[]`) from *has not run*
299:(`undefined`). ⚠️ Generalise the guard: `isEmpty`, `count` and `firstItemId` all answer
300:before there is anything to answer about.
301:
302:## Which one do I reach for?
303:
304:"Run this now and answer the user" → a cloud function, called from the app. "Every night / when a
305:record changes / retry three times then wait" → a workflow, calling cloud functions to do the work.
306:Real work — records, HTTP, mail, code — always lives in a cloud function, never in a workflow step.

# Converting "Le Gala de danse" to NodeGX — the log

The coded game is in `reference/` (plain ES modules + three.js r177). The NodeGX app is in `app/`. The rules
(`gala-rules/`) are shared, unchanged.

## Before I started

### How I read the existing code

I read it in the order the game runs: `index.html` (the page: a canvas, a top bar, a camera bar, a side sheet with
tabs/body/"go" bar, a float toolbar, a toast and a modal), `main.js` (start-up, the frame loop, pointer and keys on
the canvas), `state.js` (one shared object `G`: the save `G.S` in localStorage `gala-game-v2` plus what is on screen
now: screen, tab, picked number, the run…), then `ui.js` (752 lines: every tab is a `paint…()` function that builds
an HTML string and sets `innerHTML`, then binds `onclick`s that mutate `G.S.plan` / `G.S.school` and call
`changed()` = save + re-simulate + repaint everything), `i18n.js` (every sentence, FR/EN, many of them functions
with plurals and `<b>`), and finally the code that draws and sounds: `world.js` (three.js school, stage, loge, car
park, camera), `people.js` (dancers), `play.js` (plays the engine's schedule over time, emits "say" lines), and
`music.js` (Web Audio synth that follows the run).

The rules are already pure: `engine.js`, `data.js`, `plan.js`, `tunes.js` have no DOM and are byte-identical in
`reference/src` and `gala-rules/src` (I diffed them).

What I learned that drives the plan:

1. The UI is **"state → whole HTML string → innerHTML"** on every change. There is no component model: the "card",
   "chip", "stepper", "shop row", "verdict" are string helpers. Each one becomes a NodeGX component, and each
   `.map(...).join('')` becomes a Repeater (`For Each`) over an array.
2. All mutation goes through `changed()`, which means **one** shared store. That maps onto a NodeGX **Global
   Store** (with `persist` on for the save), so every component reads the same state without wires.
3. The 3D and the sound read `G` directly every frame. They can't become nodes (nothing in NodeGX draws three.js
   or synthesises audio), so they stay code — but they must stop reading `G`: the graph will *push* the state to
   them.
4. `i18n.js` mixes words with logic (plurals, `<b>`, conditionals). The words can be data; the logic that picks
   them stays in the code that builds each row.

### The plan: what becomes what

| coded part | becomes in NodeGX | why |
|---|---|---|
| `index.html` layout, `style.css` look | `Pages/Game`: Groups for the top bar, camera bar, side sheet, toast, intro dialog; the project's design tokens set to the theatre palette (plum, gold, velvet) | every visible element must be a node |
| `state.js` (`G.S`, save/load/mend) | a persisted **Global Store** `save` (the save) + a non-persisted Global Store `ui` (tab, screen, picks); a small "Mend save" Function on start-up that calls `gala-rules/plan.js` | state must live in nodes; the mend calls rules code |
| `ui.js` tab painters | one component per tab (`Tabs/Order`, `Tabs/Formation`, `Tabs/Gouter`, `Tabs/Costumes`, `Tabs/Build`, `Tabs/Parking`, `Tabs/Shop`, `Tabs/Notebook`), the run sheet, the results | one named section = one component |
| string helpers (`stepper`, `card`, chips, `facts`, meters, shop `row`, verdict `card`) | shared components in `UI/` (Chip, Stepper, Fact, Meter, OrderCard, ItemButton, ShopRow, Verdict…), drawn by Repeaters | repetition is data |
| `onclick` handlers that mutate the plan | each row publishes a click; the tab wires it to a small Function that returns the new plan, written back with **Set Global Store** | the nested plan edit (splice a card, clamp a time) is the code part; the wiring is nodes |
| `i18n.js` words | a **Static Data** table of words (key, fr, en) in the App, read by the view Functions; the sentences with numbers in them are templates in that table | words are data, not code |
| `engine.js` / `data.js` / `plan.js` / `tunes.js` | **project script files** `scripts/rules/*.js`, generated mechanically from `gala-rules/src` (only `import`/`export` lines rewritten to the script-file form); called from Functions with `Scripts.engine.simulate(…)` | the brief says to use them as they are; NodeGX script files are CommonJS-style, so a generator keeps them identical |
| `world.js`, `people.js`, `play.js`, `music.js` (three.js, Web Audio) | script files wrapped as factories that receive `THREE`, `window` and `document` from one **Function** node ("3D stage"), which mounts the renderer's canvas in a Group | no node draws 3D or makes sound; the brief allows this |
| `main.js` pointer handling on the canvas | stays inside the 3D code (it is input *on the canvas*) and reports taps to the graph as events | |
| run playback's feed / toasts / "done" | the 3D code sends **events** (`Noodl.Events`) that **Receive Event** nodes turn into store writes | the graph, not the code, decides what the screen shows |
| `confirm()` / `prompt()` dialogs | NodeGX popups / inline Text Input | browser dialogs are not nodes |
| the grown-ups' settings (new) | `Pages/Grownups` + a backend collection `GameChange` + cloud functions that check every change | must survive a cleared browser and another computer; a child must not be able to bypass the checks |

### What stays code, and why

- the rules (gala-rules), called from Functions — required by the brief;
- the three.js view and its pointer handling, and the Web Audio music — no node does this;
- small Functions that turn the save + the rules' answer into rows for the Repeaters, and the plan edits.
  Everything a row *shows* is a node; the Function only decides *which* rows and *what text*.

### Safety, decided up front

- The settings page needs a grown-up account. The first account made claims the `grownup` role; after that, no
  other account can (checked in a cloud function, not in the page).
- Writes go only through a cloud function that accepts known tables and known fields, clamps every number to a
  sensible range, accepts names only as short plain text from a word filter (FR + EN), and picks icons/styles/themes
  only from lists the game already knows. The collection itself is closed to direct writes.
- The browser checks the same rules again before laying a change over the game, so a bad row can never reach the
  screen even if it got into the database some other way.

---

## As I went

content.text: {"name":"drive_page","description":"Render this project from disk in a headless browser, run a list of steps on it, and report one row per step — so you can prove a button, a form or a game WORKS, not just that it draws. Each call is a fresh browser: nothing carries over from the last call. Steps (each an object with one verb): {tap: T}, {type: \"text\", into?: T, replace?: true} (appends to what the field holds unless replace), {key: \"Enter\"}, {wait_for: {text|testid|selector|url|expression}, timeout_ms?}, {read: {text: T}|{look: T}|{variable: name}|{storage: key}|{url: true}|{stub: path}|{expression}, expect?: value|{contains}} — {look: T} is what a person sees once it settles: {visible, backgroundName: \"green\", colorName, …}, and its expect names only what matters ({backgroundName: \"green\"}) — or, as lists so far, {console_errors: true}|{network_errors: true}|{other_origins: true} (expect [] = none yet), {navigate: \"/route\"}, {viewport: \"phone\"|\"390x844\"}, {screenshot: name}, {seed_storage: {key: value}} or {seed_storage: \"key\", edit: \"js changing v\"} (applied again on the next load, before the app can overwrite it), {clear_storage: true}, {stub_route: \"/api/x\", json?, body?, status?} (answers that path itself; put it first to meet a fetch made at boot), {reduced_motion: true|false}, {reload: true} (reload THIS page, as a person does), {watch: {look: T or [T, T, …]}, for_ms?, expect?: {never: {backgroundName: \"green\"}}} (every state each T showed DURING a change — a look waits for it to settle and misses a moment's flash; watch EVERY answer, not one: a colour left over lands by position). A target T is {text: \"exact label\"} or {text_contains} (a field's placeholder counts), {testid} (a data-testid set in the node's Data Attributes list — NOT its node id) or {selector}; a bare string is exact text. A tap is a real pointer press at the element's centre and is REFUSED when something else covers it, naming what a finger would hit; it answers once any scroll it started has stopped (≤2 s). The first failing step stops the run.","inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"steps":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"object","additionalProperties":{}},"minItems":1,"maxItems":60,"description":"The steps, in order. content.text: {"id":"agent-store-shared-state","title":"Shared state: one store read by two unrelated components","description":"Two components that are not parent and child, sharing state through a named store instead of prop drilling or a Send/Receive Event pair. Sign In writes `user` with Set Global Store; Header declares the same store by name and renders `state` — no wiring runs between the two components, because naming the store is what connects them. Header also subscribes to just the `user` key, so a write to any other key does not wake it, and uses `previousValue` against `value` to fire only on the signed-out → signed-in transition rather than on every change. So the 3D code can report the evening back into the graph. Wrong the first time: I passed the Function's `uses` as a JSON array; NodeGX wants one comma-separated string. And a `String` node has `saveValue`, not `set`. The server refused both writes and named the fix, so nothing broke. ### 2. The rules: `gala-rules/src/*.js` → `app/scripts/rules/*.js` - **Was:** four ES modules with `import`/`export`. - **Became:** four NodeGX script files. NodeGX script files are CommonJS-style (`exports`, and `use('rules/data')` to reach another file), so `tools/sync-rules.mjs` copies the files and rewrites only the `import`/`export` lines. Every other line is gala-rules' own. `tools/check-rules.mjs` loads the copy the way NodeGX does and checks it plays exactly the same evening as gala-rules for 4 seasons × 3 modes, and the same tunes. `npm test` in `gala-rules/` still passes; I changed nothing there. - **Didn't map cleanly:** "use them as they are" and "NodeGX script files have no `import`" pull in opposite directions. A generator + an equality check is my answer: the rules are byte-for-byte the same apart from module syntax, and re-running one command picks up a new gala-rules. ### 3. The words: `i18n.js` → a Static Data table + one small template filler - **Was:** an object of ~350 FR/EN entries, a third of them functions (`(n) => \`${n} poste${n > 1 ? 's' : ''}\``), some with `` inside. - **Became:** 389 rows `{ key, fr, en }` for a **Static Data** node (`tools/extract-words.mjs` produced them by calling each sentence function with `{0}`, `{1}`… as its arguments). Plurals became `{0:s}`, lower-casing `{0:lower}`; the ~25 functions with real logic (a sentence that changes with the floor, the season, a count) became two rows each (`say_floorSwap_bois` / `_tapis`), written by hand. `scripts/game/text.js` (56 lines) fills a template and formats times, durations and numbers. - **Lost:** the bold words inside sentences (`21 h`). A Text node draws plain text, and building HTML is exactly what the brief rules out. The sentences read the same; the emphasis is gone. ### 4. The screens' logic: `ui.js` → `scripts/view/*.js` (rows) and `scripts/game/actions.js` (presses) - **Was:** 752 lines in which each tab's painter computes what to show, *and* writes it as an HTML string, *and* binds the clicks, *and* mutates the plan inside the click handler. - **Became:** two halves of code, so the third — the screen — can be nodes: - `view/frame.js`, `view/prep.js`, `view/formation.js`, `view/run.js`: one function per tab that returns plain rows (`{ id, label, pressed, dot }` for a chip, `{ id, name, dur, locked }` for a programme card…). These are the painters with the HTML taken out; a row has exactly the fields its row component declares. - `game/actions.js`: every handler as a pure function `(save, ui, …) → { save, ui, toast }`. Nothing in it touches the page; the graph writes what comes back into the stores. - `game/save.js`: `state.js`'s fresh / mend / round-1 import, without localStorage (the store persists itself). - `tools/check-views.mjs` runs every view and action in Node for seasons 1–5 in both languages, including a played gala, and reports any word key that has no row. It found nothing missing, which surprised me; the extraction had kept the keys' shape. - **Didn't map cleanly:** the stage plan was an SVG with draggable circles. NodeGX has no SVG node for that, so `view/formation.js` computes each dancer's place in **pixels** on a 340 px plan and the graph will draw it with absolutely-positioned Groups inside **Drag** nodes. The ruler (a draggable, rotatable SVG ruler) is the one thing I chose not to rebuild; the metre marks along the plan's edges stay. ### 5. The 3D view and the music: `world.js`, `people.js`, `play.js`, `music.js` → `scripts/stage/*.js` - **Was:** modules that import three.js, read the global `G` every frame, find `#gl` in the page, and draw their textures on `document.createElement('canvas')`. - **Became:** the same code as factories, generated by `tools/sync-stage.mjs`: `exports.create(env)` receives three.js, the window and a `G` of its own. The texture canvases became `OffscreenCanvas` (never on the page), and the renderer makes its own canvas, which the "3D stage" Function puts into its Group — the only element any code places. `scripts/stage/stage.js` is the hand-written glue that was `main.js` plus the camera/run half of `ui.js`. The graph calls `sync(save, ui)` whenever a store changes; the stage answers through `emit()`: the live evening four times a second, a tap that places a piece of furniture, the camera's state, where the floating toolbar should be. - **Didn't map cleanly:** `G` was shared by the sheet and the 3D. Now there are two copies: the graph's (the stores) and the stage's, refreshed by `sync()`. The stage never changes the save itself: a tap that places a bench is sent to the graph as `place`, which runs the same action a button would. EOF

The ruler (a draggable, rotatable SVG ruler) is the one thing I chose not to rebuild; the metre marks along the plan's edges stay. ### 5. The 3D view and the music: `world.js`, `people.js`, `play.js`, `music.js` → `scripts/stage/*.js` - **Was:** modules that import three.js, read the global `G` every frame, find `#gl` in the page, and draw their textures on `document.createElement('canvas')`. - **Became:** the same code as factories, generated by `tools/sync-stage.mjs`: `exports.create(env)` receives three.js, the window and a `G` of its own. The texture canvases became `OffscreenCanvas` (never on the page), and the renderer makes its own canvas, which the "3D stage" Function puts into its Group — the only element any code places. `scripts/stage/stage.js` is the hand-written glue that was `main.js` plus the camera/run half of `ui.js`. The graph calls `sync(save, ui)` whenever a store changes; the stage answers through `emit()`: the live evening four times a second, a tap that places a piece of furniture, the camera's state, where the floating toolbar should be. - **Didn't map cleanly:** `G` was shared by the sheet and the 3D. Now there are two copies: the graph's (the stores) and the stage's, refreshed by `sync()`. The stage never changes the save itself: a tap that places a bench is sent to the graph as `place`, which runs the same action a button would. EOF
